message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical, Chemical, and Nuclear Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %), H‑3 (tritium, trace) |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first ionization) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, meaning it does not readily accept an extra electron) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| **Physical State (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (121 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Diffusivity | Extremely high (≈0.61 cm² s⁻¹ at 25 °C) |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0008 M) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Molecular form | H₂ (diatomic) |
| | Bond type | Covalent (single σ bond) |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Flammability | Highly flammable; explosive mixture with air (4–75 % H₂ in air) |
| | Reactivity | Forms hydrides with metals; reacts with halogens (forming HX) and oxygen (forming H₂O) under appropriate conditions |
| | Acidic/Basic behavior | Acts as a weak acid (H⁺ donor) in very basic solutions; can form hydride ions (H⁻) in strong bases |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as H⁻) |
| | Redox potential | Standard reduction potential of H⁺/H₂ = 0 V (by definition) |
| | Catalytic behavior | Used as a catalyst or reactant in many industrial processes (e.g., Haber-Bosch, steam reforming) |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Proton number | 1 |
| | Neutron number | 0 (protium), 1 (deuterium), 2 (tritium) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.792847 µ_N (protium), 0 (deuterium), 5.586 µ_N (tritium) |
| | Half‑life (tritium) | 12.32 years |
| | Decay mode (tritium) | β⁻ decay to helium‑3 |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen) |
| | Industrial | Production of ammonia (Haber-Bosch), methanol, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage in metal hydrides, high‑pressure tanks |
| | Scientific | Calibration gas, tracer studies, neutron sources (via tritium) |
| | Environmental | Clean combustion (produces only water vapor) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Explosion limits in air | Lower limit 4 %, upper limit 75 % |
| | Combustion temperature | 500–600 °C (ignition) |
| | Storage pressure | Up to 700 bar (compressed gas) or cryogenic temperatures for liquid hydrogen |
| | Health hazards | Low toxicity, but inhalation can displace oxygen → hypoxia; tritium is radioactive |

---

### Quick Summary

- **Hydrogen is the lightest element** (atomic number 1) and exists naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂) at room temperature.
- It has **three stable isotopes**: protium (most common), deuterium (stable heavy isotope), and tritium (radioactive).
- Physically, it is **colorless, odorless, tasteless, and extremely light** (density ≈ 0.09 g L⁻¹ at STP).
- Chemically, it is **highly reactive**: it forms covalent bonds, reacts explosively with air, and can act as both an acid (H⁺) and a base (H⁻) depending on the environment.
- Its **nuclear properties** make it useful in nuclear science (tritium as a beta emitter) and in fusion research.
- Hydrogen’s **low environmental impact** (combustion yields only water) makes it a key candidate for clean energy technologies, though its handling requires careful safety measures due to flammability and, in the case of tritium, radioactivity.
